title: Unify async IO surface and KV rehydration pipeline to reduce tail latency
creator: Ava Patel
description:
Background: The serving runtime currently implements two divergent code paths for fetching tokenized context and model KV state: (1) the legacy synchronous rehydration on scheduler threads and (2) the newer async disk/network rehydrate helpers used by the continuous-batcher hotpath. Over time this divergence caused duplicated logic, inconsistent backpressure behavior, and several sources of tail latency: blocking scheduler worker threads during cold rehydrates, duplicated allocations and memcpy, and inconsistent prioritization of urgent rehydrate requests.

Goal: Replace the two ad-hoc rehydration paths with a single asynchronous IO surface and a sharded rehydration pipeline that: (A) keeps scheduler threads non-blocking, (B) applies a single admission/backpressure policy across disk+network rehydrates, (C) merges small I/O reads to reduce syscall overhead, and (D) exposes backpressure and latency metrics for rollout.

Outcome: Improve p99 token fetch latency by 30% on mixed workloads, reduce scheduler CPU stalls, and simplify code paths to make future KV consistency/replication work easier.
acceptance_criteria: Unified async_io::Rehydrate API implemented and documented
No scheduler threads perform blocking disk/network IO in the critical fastpath (verified by runtime tracing)
End-to-end p99 token fetch latency improves by >= 25% on the standard benchmark (stable-load-64) compared to current main
New pipeline has feature-flagged rollout with automated health checks and rollback path
All existing unit/integration tests pass and new regression tests for concurrent rehydrate scenarios added
testing_plan: Unit tests for async_io adapter and mock disk/network layer
Integration test: mixed-batch benchmark w/ and w/o cold KV hits (automated in CI)
Chaos test: randomly delay disk reads to validate prioritization and backpressure
Long-run soak: 48h stable-load-64 to verify no memory growth or GC spikes
rollout_plan: Canary: enable 5% of production traffic for 6 hours, monitor token fetch p50/p95/p99 and scheduler goroutine/thread blocking counts
Ramp to 25% for 12 hours if no regressions, then 100% over 24 hours
Rollback immediately if p99 or CPU stalls regress beyond thresholds defined in the health checks
risks: Concurrency bugs when consolidating two code paths could cause deadlocks or data races
Regression in cold-start performance if batching/merge windows are tuned incorrectly
Dependency upgrade risk: plan includes upgrading async runtime (tokio-like) which may change scheduling semantics
Observability gaps: new pipeline must expose sufficient traces/labels to debug regressions quickly
notes_and_tradeoffs: We considered a fully synchronous rewrite of the rehydrate path but rejected it because it would not eliminate scheduler blocking and would increase latency variance
Opted for a sharded worker pool with priority queues instead of a single global priority queue to avoid head-of-line blocking under high concurrency
Deferred adoption of kernel-level io_uring until after rollout to reduce scope; will evaluate in follow-up task if merged_io_ratio remains low
